characterList.description: A middle-aged man with dark hair, wearing a navy blue suit and a patterned tie. He is a news anchor hosting the show.
characterList.name: Chris Wallace

characterList.description: An older man with white hair, wearing a dark suit and a light blue tie. He is the former president of the United States.
characterList.name: Bill Clinton

content_metadata.description: A detailed breakdown of the interview between Chris Wallace and Bill Clinton, focusing on post-presidency work and the response to 9/11.

qAndA.answer: He mentions attempts to stop the genocide in Kosovo, make peace in the Middle East, and pass a budget that provides after-school programs and increased college aid.
qAndA.question: What specific examples does Bill Clinton provide of actions he took as President to address terrorism?

qAndA.answer: Initially, his demeanor is relaxed and he maintains eye contact with the interviewer. As the conversation shifts to 9/11, he becomes increasingly animated, using more hand gestures, his voice gets louder, and at times he looks away.
qAndA.question: How does Bill Clinton's body language change throughout the interview?

qAndA.answer: He seems to be implying that his decision to stay in Somalia demonstrates his commitment to addressing global issues even in the face of risk and opposition.
qAndA.question: What is the subtext of Clinton's repeated emphasis on the fact that everyone wanted him to withdraw from Somalia?

qAndA.answer: The flowers symbolize an attempt at civility and decorum, contrasting with the heated nature of the exchange.
qAndA.question: What is the symbolic meaning of the flower arrangement placed between Clinton and Wallace during the interview?

qAndA.answer: Clinton emphasizes that he acted responsibly against Bin Laden based on the information available, defending his legacy against politically motivated criticisms.
qAndA.question: What is the overall message Clinton is trying to convey about his actions as President regarding Bin Laden?

activities.description: Chris Wallace introduces the interview with former President Clinton, highlighting his recent Global Initiative Forum. Video footage of Bill Clinton speaking at the forum is shown.
Chris Wallace sets the stage for the interview, outlining the agreed-upon ground rules and hinting at an unexpected turn of events.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Sets the stage for Clinton's interview on post-presidency work and 9/11 response.

narrativeProgression.description: The introduction sets the stage by highlighting Bill Clinton's global initiative work and the significance of this interview being his first on Fox News Sunday.
Wallace teases viewers by mentioning that the interview did not go as planned, setting up suspense for the actual exchange.

scenes.thematicElements: Introduction to Clinton’s Global Initiative and interview setup.
scenes.title: Introduction to Interview

videoEditingDetails.description: Video transitions from Chris Wallace in the studio to footage of Bill Clinton's Global Initiative Forum. Text overlays indicating 'FRIDAY' and 'NEW YORK' appear.

activities.description: Chris Wallace welcomes Bill Clinton to the show and asks him about his motivation for helping developing countries, referencing a quote from The New Yorker.
Bill Clinton answers the question, detailing his commitment to doing good and expressing his passion for his current work.
Wallace asks Clinton to compare the power he had as president to what he can achieve now as a former president.
Clinton explains the wider scope of power he had as president but emphasizes the freedom he has now to focus on specific issues without being swayed by unexpected events.

Wallace shifts the conversation to 9/11 and asks why Clinton didn't do more to stop Bin Laden. Clinton addresses the context of the question, highlighting the political climate and criticisms he received both during and after his presidency.

characterInteraction.description: The interaction begins politely but deteriorates into a clash as Wallace questions Clinton about 9/11.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Delves into Clinton's post-presidency impact and media scrutiny on 9/11 handling.

mood.description: Starts as Calm and transitions to Angry

narrativeProgression.description: The interview initially focuses on Clinton's current work and motivations, establishing his commitment to global development and emphasizing his personal satisfaction.
The introduction of 9/11 shifts the narrative towards past events and potential failures during Clinton's presidency.
The interview quickly escalates into a heated debate about responsibility for 9/11, with Clinton defensively refuting accusations and challenging the interviewer's line of questioning.

scenes.title: The Interview with Bill Clinton

climax.description: Clinton's heated defense of his actions regarding Bin Laden, leading to a dramatic confrontation with Wallace.

storylines.description: Analysis of Clinton's career and media portrayal in the context of terrorism.

dollars was pledged to tackle some of the worst problems in developing countries, such as
poverty, disease, and climate change.
As part of the conference, Mr. Clinton agreed to his first one-on-one interview ever on Fox
News Sunday.
The ground rules were simple.
15 minutes for our sit-down split evenly between the global initiative and anything else
we wanted to ask.
But as you'll see now in the full, unedited interview, that's not how it turned out.
This president welcomed to Fox News Sunday.
Thanks.
In a recent issue of the New Yorker, you say, quote, I'm 60 years old and I damn near
died and I'm worried about how many lives I can save before I do die.
Is that what drives you in your effort to help in these developing countries?
Yes, I really, but I don't mean that sounds sort of morbid when you say it like that.
I mean, I actually, yes.
But yeah, but the way I said it, the tone in which I said it was actually almost whimsical
and humorous, that is, this is what I love to do.
It is what I think I should do.
That is, I have had a wonderful life.
I got to be president.
I got to live the life of my dreams.
I dodged a bullet with that heart problem.
And I really think I should, I think I owe it to my fellow countrymen and people throughout
the world to spend time saving lives, solving problems, helping people see the future.
But as it happens, I love it.
I mean, I feel it's a great gift.
It's a rewarding way to spend my life.
Someone asked you and I don't want, again, to be too morbid.
This is what you said.
He asked you if you could wind up doing more good as a former president than as a president.
And you said, only if I live a long time.
Yeah, that's true.
How do you rate, compare the powers of being in office as president and what you can do
out of office as a former president?
Well, when you are president, you can operate on a much broader scope.
So for example, you can simultaneously be trying to stop a genocide in Kosovo, you know,
make peace in the Middle East, pass a budget that gives millions of kids a chance to have
after-school programs and has a huge increase in college aid at home.
In other words, you got a lot of different moving parts and you can move them all at once.
But you're also more at the mercy of events.
That is, President Bush did not run for president to deal with 9-11.
But once it happened, it wasn't as if he had an option.
Once I looked at the economic, I'll give you a much more mundane example.
Once I looked at the economic data, the new data, after I won the election, I realized
that I would have to work much harder to reduce the deficit and therefore I would have less
money in my first year to invest in things I want to invest in.
So what is it that you can do as a former president?
So what you can do as a former president is you don't have the wide range of power.
So you have to concentrate on fewer things.
But you are less at the mercy of unfolding events.
So if I say, look, we're going to work on the economic empowerment of poor people on fighting

people and on trying to avoid the worst calamities of climate change and help to revitalize the
economy in the process.
I can actually do that.
I mean, because tomorrow, when I get up, if there's a bad headline in the paper, it's

That's the joy of being a former president.
And it is true that if you live long enough and you really have great discipline in the
way you do this, like this CGI, you might be able to affect as many lives or more for
the good as you did as president.
When we announced that you were going to be on Fox News Sunday, I got a lot of email
